appendix.title: The rxgk security class
appendix.para: This chapter explains and describes how to set up the rxgk security class, a new feature in OpenAFS. Note that rxgk support is currently experimental and various options and behaviors are subject to change; this chapter describes just the current implementation in OpenAFS as it exists right now.

sect1.title: Background
sect1.para: Current releases of OpenAFS (versions 1.8.x and earlier) use the rxkad security class for authenticated and encrypted network traffic. rxkad is originally derived from krb4, with various additions and extensions to allow it to be used with krb5 and non-DES long-term keys. But rxkad still always uses a DES-based encryption algorithm called fcrypt on the wire, with no way to specify other algorithms.

The rxgk security class is intended as the replacement for rxkad, and is intended to be useable with any encryption supported by the underlying platform. This offers better security, but also better performance, as modern cryptography algorithms tend to be much faster, especially with hardware acceleration.

The rxgk security class also has a number of other features and improvements:
It is not restricted to Kerberos; anything supporting the GSS-API can be used. However, OpenAFS currently only supports rxgk with krb5 for now.
Fileservers can run with per-fileserver credentials, instead of every server needing to have the same cell-wide secret key in KeyFileExt. OpenAFS does not support this yet; all fileservers must have the cell-wide key in KeyFileExt.
Client machines can have per-client credentials, which are used together with per-user credentials. This can allow you to use host-based access control that uses actual credentials, instead of the inconsistent IP-based "machine entries" in the ptdb. OpenAFS does not support this yet.
Various other improvements related to security, stability, and performance that are not directly visible to an administrator.

Even though OpenAFS does not support some of these features right now, it can be helpful to know that they exist; so you know not to try to use them, and so you know what may change in future releases.

rxgk also provides a way for a client to securely ask a vlserver whether a fileserver supports rxgk or not. This allows for rxgk to be deployed gradually in a cell, but it means that each fileserver must tell a vlserver that it supports rxgk.

sect1.title: Building
sect1.para: When building OpenAFS, run ./configure with the flags --enable-rxgk --enable-pthreaded-bos, which will turn on rxgk for all components. You will need GSS headers and libraries installed, which may be separate packages from your krb5 libraries.
rxgk is tested most on Linux-based platforms with MIT krb5, but other platforms should also work. If you encounter build issues, please let us know.
Once binaries have been built, you can install them like normal. If you have an existing rxkad-based setup, you can verify that everything still works before proceeding with setting up rxgk.

sect1.title: Basic Localauth Setup
sect1.para: First, we'll setup the cell-wide rxgk secret key. This allows us to use rxgk when using the -localauth option for most commands, but server processes won't use this for internal communication yet.

Run the following on a server to generate a random cell-wide secret key with kvno 1 and store it in your KeyFileExt:
# asetkey add-random rxgk 1 Added random key with type 1 kvno 1 subtype 17
Distribute that KeyFileExt to all servers in the cell, like normal. Remember to either restart the server processes or touch CellServDB so the server processes notice the updated KeyFileExt.
Now we can check that -localauth access works by running some commands. Run these commands with -rxgk crypt to use rxgk, and make sure no other error messages appear.

Verify that the key works with the ptserver:
# pts examine system:administrators -localauth -rxgk crypt Name: system:administrators, id: -204, owner: system:administrators, creator: system:administrators, membership: 1, flags: S-M--, group quota: unlimited.
If you see an error message like Could not get afs tokens, running unauthenticated, then something is wrong.

Verify that the key works with the vlserver:
# vos listvldb root.cell -localauth -rxgk crypt
root.cell RWrite: 536870912 ROnly: 536870913 Backup: 536870914 number of sites -> 2 server fs1.example.com partition /vicepa RW Site server fs1.example.com partition /vicepa RO Site
If you see an error message like Could not get afs tokens, running unauthenticated, then something is wrong.

Verify that the key works with the volserver:
# vos listpart localhost -localauth -verbose -rxgk crypt -rxgk-novldb The partitions on the server are: /vicepa /vicepb Total: 2
If you see an error message like Could not get afs tokens, running unauthenticated, then something is wrong.

Note the use of the flag -rxgk-novldb. This tells vos to not negotiate per-server rxgk tokens from the VLDB. We use this flag because we haven't setup the VLDB for rxgk yet; later on, after the VLDB is setup, you won't need to use that flag anymore.

Verify that the key works with the bosserver:
# bos status localhost -localauth -rxgk crypt -rxgk-cellwide Instance ptserver, currently running normally. Instance vlserver, currently running normally. Instance dafs, currently running normally. Auxiliary status is: file server running.
If you see an error message like bos: running unauthenticated, then something is wrong.

Note the use of the flag -rxgk-cellwide. This tells bos to use the rxgk cell-wide key from KeyFileExt instead of GSS authentication, since we haven't configured bosserver GSS credentials yet. Later on, after GSS credentials have been configured, you don't need to use that flag anymore.
You can also run privileged commands to prove that you are authenticated as an administrator. For example, pts createuser or vos create.

sect1.title: Server-to-server Localauth Setup
sect1.para: At this point, the server processes are still using rxkad to talk to the other servers. To use rxgk for server-to-server traffic, give the option -s2scrypt rxgk-crypt to the ptserver, vlserver, and fileserver.

Doing this for the ptserver and vlserver is optional (but recommended, of course, to get the benefits of rxgk), and meaningless if you only have one dbserver in the cell. Doing this for the fileserver is required for clients to be able to use rxgk for that fileserver, since this is how the vlserver knows whether a fileserver supports rxgk or not.

To do this, issue the bos delete and bos create commands to recreate the relevant bnodes. See Starting the Database Server Processes or "Creating and Removing Processes" in the Admin Guide. This can be done one server (or one process) at a time, or the whole cell at once.

For example, you should see something like this after the relevant flags have been added:
# bos status localhost -long -localauth -rxgk crypt -rxgk-cellwide Instance ptserver, (type is simple) currently running normally. Process last started at Sat May 11 23:44:44 2024 (1 proc starts) Command 1 is '/usr/afs/bin/ptserver -s2scrypt rxgk-crypt'
Instance vlserver, (type is simple) currently running normally. Process last started at Sat May 11 23:44:44 2024 (1 proc starts) Command 1 is '/usr/afs/bin/vlserver -s2scrypt rxgk-crypt'
Instance dafs, (type is dafs) currently running normally. Auxiliary status is: file server running. Process last started at Sat May 11 23:44:44 2024 (3 proc starts) Command 1 is '/usr/afs/bin/dafileserver -s2scrypt rxgk-crypt' Command 2 is '/usr/afs/bin/davolserver' Command 3 is '/usr/afs/bin/salvageserver' Command 4 is '/usr/afs/bin/dasalvager'
To check that server processes are actually using rxgk for server-to-server traffic, you can use rxdebug and see what security class is being used for the client connections to other servers.

For example, for the ptserver:
# rxdebug localhost 7002 -onlyclient -allconnections Connection from host 192.0.2.10, port 7002, Cuid d34db33f/deadbeef serial 3, natMTU 1444, security index 4, client conn rxgk: level crypt [...]
The "security index 4" and "rxgk: level crypt" shows that the connection is using rxgk. In this example, 192.0.2.10 is another ptserver.

Do this for the ptserver (port 7002), vlserver (port 7003), and fileserver (port 7000), to verify that rxgk is being used. The ptserver will talk to other ptservers, the vlserver will talk to other vlservers, and the fileserver will talk to vlservers and ptservers.

If the fileserver is able to successfully contact the vlserver over rxgk, you should also see this message in VLLog:
Thu Apr 11 18:12:51 2024 Flagging fileserver 0010bf8a-4cfe-1d8e-a8-16-e71011acaa77 in the VLDB as supporting rxgk with the cell-wide key.

At this point, you can also run vos without the flag -rxgk-novldb. This causes vos to use per-server rxgk credentials instead of using the cell-wide rxgk key. This currently doesn't matter much because OpenAFS doesn't support per-server keys, but it's useful for testing.

For example:
# vos listpart localhost -localauth -verbose -rxgk crypt Getting rxgk creds for volserver uuid 0010bf8a-4cfe-1d8e-a8-16-e71011acaa77... done. The partitions on the server are: /vicepa /vicepb Total: 2

sect1.title: Client fileserver access with krb5
sect1.para: Now that rxgk is being used by the server processes internally, we can setup rxgk to be used by users and clients to access the fileserver. To do this, we create the krb5 principal afs-rxgk/_afs.<cell>, and extract a keytab for that principal to /usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab on your dbservers.

However, note that clients may detect the existence of the afs-rxgk/_afs.<cell> principal as an indication that the cell supports rxgk. So, if you create that principal on your KDC, clients may immediately think that the cell supports rxgk, but using rxgk will fail until you distribute rxgk.keytab to the vlservers. The instructions provided here ignore this problem, but there are ways to avoid this. You can generate the keytab before creating the principal on the KDC, or you can create the principal on the KDC without allowing it to be used by clients. See your KDC documentation for details, or you may find the similar procedures in the OpenAFS document how-to-rekey.txt helpful.
Ignoring those issues, the first step is to create the krb5 principal afs-rxgk/_afs.<cell>, such as afs-rxgk/_afs.example.com.

For example, with MIT krb5:
# kadmin.local kadmin.local: add_principal -randkey afs-rxgk/_afs.example.com Principal "afs-rxgk/_afs.example.com@EXAMPLE.COM" created. kadmin.local: ktadd -k /usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab -norandkey afs-rxgk/_afs.example.com Entry for principal afs-rxgk/_afs.example.com with kvno 1, encryption type aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab WRFILE:/usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab. Entry for principal afs-rxgk/_afs.example.com with kvno 1, encryption type aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab WRFILE:/usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab.

Now distribute /usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab to all dbservers, and restart the vlserver processes. Note that you should not use this keytab with asetkey; it is unrelated to the keys in KeyFileExt, KeyFile, or rxkad.keytab.

You should now see this message in VLLog when vlserver starts:
Thu Apr 11 18:19:01 2024 rxgk: Using GSS acceptor creds for afs-rxgk@_afs.example.com in /usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab
Once that has been done, you can run gklog on a client to obtain rxgk tokens. The gklog command is similar to aklog, but obtains rxgk tokens using GSS.

For example (with MIT krb5):
$ kinit Password for user@EXAMPLE.COM: $ gklog $ klist Ticket cache: KEYRING:persistent:1001:1001 Default principal: user@EXAMPLE.COM
Valid starting Expires Service principal 04/11/2024 16:11:48 04/12/2024 16:11:44 afs-rxgk/_afs.example.com@EXAMPLE.COM 04/11/2024 16:11:45 04/12/2024 16:11:44 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.COM@EXAMPLE.COM $ tokens
Tokens held by the Cache Manager:
rxgk tokens for pts id 1004 for example.com [Expires Apr 12 15:58] --End of list-- $ pts whoami -rxgk crypt Name: user@EXAMPLE.COM, id: 1004 Name data: type 2 (gss), base64 BAEACwYJKoZIhvcSAQICAAAAEHVzZXJARVhBTVBMRS5DT00=
With those tokens, you should be able to access files in AFS just like if you had rxkad tokens, as well as run pts and vos commands.

One notable difference between gklog and aklog is that gklog needs to talk to the realm's KDC and to the cell's vlservers. gklog cannot obtain rxgk tokens if it cannot reach any vlservers, This is different from aklog, which can obtain tokens without any OpenAFS servers running.

sect1.title: bosserver access with krb5
sect1.para: Communicating with bosserver using non-localauth rxgk is a bit different than for other server processes. For other server processes, the client obtains tokens by talking to the vlserver processes in a cell when you run gklog. But the vlservers may not be running when you want to run bos to bring up the vlserver processes.

So, using bos with rxgk does not use tokens obtained via gklog by default. Instead, bos negotiates rxgk tokens by talking directly to the bosserver process every time you run bos, using the user's krb5 tickets.

This is more similar to how some other non-AFS krb5 and GSS services work, and requires a service principal for each server running bosserver, and may require DNS to be set up correctly depending on your krb5 configuration.

To set this up, create a krb5 principal afs3-bos/<machine name> and extract it to /usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab on that machine. Afterwards, rxgk.keytab will contain both the afs-rxgk principal (if this is a dbserver) as well as the afs3-bos principal for that machine.

If you want to use the same rxgk.keytab file on multiple machines, it's okay for all of them to contain afs3-bos entries for other machines; each bosserver just needs at least their own afs3-bos principal in their rxgk.keytab file. It's better for security compartmentalization for each server to only have its own afs3-bos entry and not any others for other servers, but having extra entries won't break anything.

For example (with MIT krb5):
# kadmin.local kadmin.local: add_principal -randkey afs3-bos/fs1.example.com Principal "afs3-bos/fs1.example.com@EXAMPLE.COM" created. kadmin.local: ktadd -k /usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab -norandkey afs3-bos/fs1.example.com Entry for principal afs3-bos/fs1.example.com with kvno 1, encryption type aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab WRFILE:/usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab. Entry for principal afs3-bos/fs1.example.com with kvno 1, encryption type aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab WRFILE:/usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab. kadmin.local: ^D # ktutil ktutil: read_kt /usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab ktutil: list slot KVNO Principal ---- ---- --------------------------------------------------------------------- 1 1 afs-rxgk/_afs.example.com@EXAMPLE.COM 2 1 afs-rxgk/_afs.example.com@EXAMPLE.COM 3 1 afs3-bos/fs1.example.com@EXAMPLE.COM 4 1 afs3-bos/fs1.example.com@EXAMPLE.COM

And then restart the bosserver. You should now see this message in BosLog:
Thu Apr 11 18:19:01 2024 rxgk: Using GSS acceptor creds for afs3-bos@fs1 in /usr/afs/etc/rxgk.keytab

Once that is done, you should be able to use bos with -rxgk crypt without -rxgk-cellwide. But you must specify the same server name as is exists in the afs3-bos principal name (fs1, or fs1.example.com in the given example), or your krb5 library must be able to canonicalize the given address to that name. (For example, in MIT krb5, see the configuration directives dns_canonicalize_hostname and rdns.) Specifying localhost, for example, may not work.

For example:
$ bos status fs1.example.com -rxgk crypt Instance ptserver, currently running normally. Instance vlserver, currently running normally. Instance dafs, currently running normally. Auxiliary status is: file server running. $ bos status localhost -rxgk crypt gss_init_sec_context: Unspecified GSS failure. Minor code may provide more information [851968] gss_init_sec_context: Server afs3-bos/localhost@EXAMPLE.COM not found in Kerberos database [2529638919] bos: Security module structure inconsistent (configuring connection security)

You can still use localhost when using -rxgk-cellwide. That flag causes bos to use the tokens obtained by gklog (for non-localauth), or tokens generated from the cell-wide key data from KeyFileExt (if -localauth is given), and doesn't use the afs3-bos service principal to obtain tokens. This isn't the default behavior, because it may not be possible to acquire tokens if the vlserver isn't running, and in the future the target server may not have the rxgk cell-wide key available at all.

sect1.title: UserList GSS entries
sect1.para:
Existing commands to alter the UserList like bos adduser currently only work for rxkad identities. To add access to users using rxgk, you must add GSS identities to the UserList. There are no commands to do this conveniently yet, but you can still add entries to the UserList manually. For example:
# pts whoami -rxgk crypt Name: admin@EXAMPLE.COM, id: 1005 Name data: type 2 (gss), base64 BAEACwYJKoZIhvcSAQICAAAAEWFkbWluQEVYQU1QTEUuQ09N
# cat /usr/afs/etc/UserList admin 1 BAEACwYJKoZIhvcSAQICAAAAEWFkbWluQEVYQU1QTEUuQ09N admin@EXAMPLE.COM
# vos create fs1.example.com a vol.test -rxgk crypt Volume 536870991 created on partition /vicepa of fs1.example.com

The second line of the example UserList shows a gss identity (type 1), with the base64-encoded identity of the user (obtained from pts whoami), followed by the display name for that user. Note that this line starts with a space before the 1, to distinguish it from lines for rxkad users.

You may notice that the pts whoami command shows a name of "type 2" for GSS identities, but the UserList identifies a GSS user with a 1. This is confusing, but is due to certain constants in the wire protocol (PRAUTHTYPE_GSS) differing from constants in our internal file formats (RX_ID_GSS), both of which were defined many years ago.
